32.0.0.en: 1 If they make you the master of the feast, do not be lifted up, but be among them as one of them. 2 Take care of them, and then sit down, and when you have fulfilled your duty, recline, 3 that you may rejoice because of them, and receive a crown as an ornament, and be honored by their gifts. 4 Speak, you who are old, for it becomes you. 5 But with accurate knowledge, and do not hinder the music.

32.0.1.en: In ancient times the leading of a banquet was regarded as a great honor to a person. When a godly man is appointed master of the table, he sets in his heart that he is as one of all those present, marked in his dealing by a spirit of humility and care for all the invited guests, whatever their positions.

32.0.2.en: Have they appointed you master of the feast? Do not be proud, but be as one of them; take care of them, and then sit down [1].

32.0.3.en: The aim of banquets is the practice of love, the fellowship of joy, and the practice of brotherhood in a spirit of meekness. Therefore the leader of the table is bound by particular qualities, among them that he does not think himself to be in a position of authority and control over the arrangement of the table, but reckons himself one of those who share in the table, committed to kindness in a spirit of love and wisdom, and that he is invited to serve those present, not to be served.

32.1.0.en: * Behold how the leader who led them into the holy land, the land of promise, was himself one of the people. He was the successor of Moses, and yet he did not allow himself to claim a portion of the land. Although he was the leader of the people, he waited to take the small portion; he who is called Joshua (Jesus) deserved to build the place which he had received and to take care of its rebuilding, so as to make it truly fitting as a gift of God and a divine inheritance... (Joshua the son of Nun) drew lots for all and left for himself the last place. What do you think, why did he want to be the last? Surely to be first of all (Mt 19:30) [2].

32.1.1.en: Origen After fulfilling all your duties, sit at the table, that you may rejoice on their account, and receive a crown for your good leadership [2].

32.1.2.en: It befits the leader to realize his responsibilities regarding the food and its arrangement, and to observe and direct the conversation among those present, neither in unseemly jesting nor in dry seriousness. It befits him that the conversations not be sharp, but cheerful, full of love and profitable. Cheerful conversation is the crown of a table that is properly prepared. Some discussions must be postponed to their proper time, for man shall not live by bread alone (Mt 4:4).

32.1.3.en: Likewise the table is not the proper place for dry discussions.

32.2.0.en: Speak, O elder, for you are fit for it, acting with accurate knowledge, and do not hinder the music [3].

32.2.1.en: In a person's management of the leading of the banquet, it befits him that the banquet be a living icon of the supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:9), in which quiet music prevails, not noise.

32.3.0.en: 6 Do not pour out talk where there is listening, and do not bring forth wisdom out of its time. 7 The strains of singers at a banquet of wine are like a seal of ruby in a setting of gold. 8 The melodies of singers over pleasant wine are like a seal of emerald in a work of gold. 9 Listen while you are silent, and by your modesty you will gain favor. 10 Speak, young man, but seldom, when need calls you. 11 If you are asked twice, answer briefly, 12 expressing much in few words, and be as one who knows and keeps silent. 13 In the company of the great do not make yourself equal to them, and among elders do not be much given to chattering. 14 Before the thunder goes forth the lightning, and before the modest goes favor. 15 When the time has come, rise, do not delay. Hasten to your house, do not be negligent. There amuse yourself, 16 and do what you please, and do not sin by words of pride. 17 And for all these things bless your Maker, who makes you drunk with His good things.

32.3.1.en: Do not pour out talk at a gathering, and do not bring forth wisdom out of its time [4].

32.3.2.en: The table is not a field for displaying a man's eloquence, wisdom, gifts and abilities.

32.3.3.en: * In my opinion limits must be set to speech; if one wishes to practice self-control, his limit is to stop at answering the questions directed to him, even if he is able to speak.

32.3.4.en: St. Clement of Alexandria A musical gathering at a wine banquet is like a seal of ruby in a setting of gold [5].

32.3.5.en: In that Sirach prefers quiet music with a little wine, he means that an atmosphere of love and joy should prevail at the table; the table is not a place for talking of profound thoughts that are hard to follow, nor should a spirit of argument prevail there, which may turn into a kind of sharpness of style. Tertullian says: "Argument over the Holy Scriptures profits nothing. This is plain; it only wearies a man's stomach or his mind."

32.3.6.en: In the early ages Christians were forbidden to eat with heretics, perhaps for fear that the table might turn into an atmosphere of dry disputation.

32.3.7.en: A musical melody over pleasant wine is like a seal of emerald in a setting of gold [6].

32.4.0.en: Speak, young man, when need calls you, twice at the most if you are asked repeatedly [7].

32.4.1.en: He gives us commandments concerning the conduct of the young man at the banquet, for it is not an opportunity to display his cheerful personality in extremes of loud laughter and vain, unedifying talk. Ben Sirach requires him to lessen his talking at the banquet, perhaps that he may be rather a listener and so benefit from the experience of others.

32.5.0.en: Be concise, and express much in few words, and be as one who knows, yet holds his tongue [8].

32.5.1.en: Brevity in speech during the meal is effective and practical. Much talking, whatever the subject of the conversation, scatters the mind, especially at the table. The less the young man talks, the more he becomes an object of the esteem and admiration of those present, especially since the great and the elders do not tend to listen for long.

32.5.2.en: * Let these take heed that when the young of birds try to fly before their wings have grown strong, they fall from above where they were trying to soar. Likewise let them understand that if we place heavy timbers upon the frames of buildings that have not yet become strong, the result is not the living of a life but destruction and death.

32.5.3.en: Likewise when women bear children whose growth is not complete, they fill graves with the dead, not houses with life. Therefore the Truth Himself teaches His disciples about the power of teaching, He who wished to give an example to His followers not to venture upon the ministry of teaching before their ability for it is complete. And He who could have given strength at once to the one whom He wished to strengthen added at once, saying: "But tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high" (Lk 24:49).

32.5.4.en: To remain in the city means to withdraw into seclusion between ourselves and our own souls, so that we do not go about as teachers unless we have put on divine power. Only then do we go outside from meditation in the depths of our souls to where we can teach others. Therefore it is said by the tongue of the wise man: "Speak, young man, but seldom, when need calls you. If you are asked twice, answer briefly" (cf. Sir 32:10-11).

32.5.5.en: For this reason our Savior Himself, who is the Creator and who sits in the heavens, continually teaching the angels by the declaration of His surpassing power, did not wish to be a teacher of men on earth before the age of thirty. And it is clear that He wished to instill a holy fear in those who are hasty, when they see that He who was without sin did not come forward to teach with the grace of the perfect life until He reached the fullness of age. And here the Gospels show: "And when he was twelve years old... the child Jesus tarried behind in Jerusalem" (Lk 2:42-43). And when His parents sought Him, "they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions" (Lk 2:46) [3].

32.6.0.en: In the company of the great, do not make yourself equal to them, and if another speaks, lessen your talk [9].

32.6.1.en: Lightning flashes before the thunder, and favors [4] go before the humble man [10].

32.6.2.en: The banquet is a wonderful opportunity to show love in a spirit of humility, without expecting words of praise from those present.

32.6.3.en: * If we bear the holy thought of God like a seal that is not loosened, it is imprinted upon our hearts by constant, pure remembrance. By this we become partakers in the love of God, who inspires us to fulfill the commandments of the Lord, and He Himself remains kept in us without distraction [5].

32.6.4.en: * This is a testimony that no one can deny, that if we fulfilled all the rites and works of righteousness, and kept all the commandments of the Lord, and performed great wonders without love, they would be counted as works of iniquity and not as gifts of the Spirit, not because there is anything faulty in these works themselves, but because those who perform them have as their whole aim to magnify themselves, as the Apostle says of those who "suppose that godliness is a means of gain" (1 Tim 6:5). And in another place he says: "Some indeed preach Christ even of envy and strife; and some also of good will: the one preach Christ of contention, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my bonds" (Phil 1:15-16). And in another place he affirms: "For neither at any time used we flattering words, as ye know, nor a cloke of covetousness; God is witness: nor of men sought we glory, neither of you, nor yet of others, when we were able to be in dignity as the apostles of Christ" (1 Thess 2:5-6) [6].

32.6.5.en: * Each time we bend the knee and rise, we show by this act that sin throws us to the ground, and the love of Christ calls us to heaven [7].

32.6.6.en: St. Basil the Great * What is the head of the virtues? Humility! Therefore (the Lord Christ) began with it, saying: "Blessed are the poor" (Mt 5:3; Lk 6:20). This head has no long lock of hair, nor hair in curls, but in it is beauty, so that it draws God to it. Of it He says: "To this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word" (Isa 66:2); and "Mine eyes are upon the meek of the earth" (cf. Ps 101:6); and "The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart" (Ps 34:18)... This is the parent of wisdom. When one has it, he has the rest of the virtues also... It pours out great beauty even upon the other members. If someone mixed endless colors, they would not bring about such beauty [8].

32.6.7.en: St. John Chrysostom Rise to leave the place at a fitting time, and do not linger.

32.7.0.en: Hasten to your house and do not be slothful [11].

32.7.1.en: He calls us to observe the sanctification of time, so that lingering and excess in staying up late are not fitting, out of care for a person's health. On the other hand it is fitting that the banquet not be at the expense of the family's joy, especially the children's, or at the expense of a person's worship in his house. Recreation at home is better than staying up late at parties.

32.8.0.en: There you will be glad, and do what seems good to you, but do not sin by words of pride [12].

32.9.0.en: And bless your Creator for all these things, who fills you with His good things [13].

32.9.1.en: If it is necessary to open the banquet with prayer, that the Lord may bless the food and lead those present to joy of spirit in His divine presence even while eating, it befits a person to offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving for the joyful spiritual atmosphere he has enjoyed.

32.10.0.en: 18 He who fears the Lord will accept His discipline, and those who rise early for Him will find His favor. 19 He who seeks the Law will be filled with it, but the hypocrite will stumble in it. 20 Those who fear the Lord will find justice, and will kindle from judgments a lamp for themselves. 21 The sinful man avoids reproof, and finds arguments that suit his desire. 22 The man of counsel does not neglect reflection, but the proud, who is not such a one, is not seized by fear, 23 not even after he has done as he pleased without counsel. 24 Do nothing without counsel, and you will not regret your deed. 25 Do not walk in the way of ruin, and you will not stumble over the stones. Do not cast yourself on a path that you have not tried, lest you make for yourself a stumblingblock. 26 Beware even of your sons, and be on guard against the members of your household. 27 In all your works follow your conscience, for that is the keeping of the commandments. 28 He who follows the Law keeps the commandments, and he who trusts in the Lord will not lose.

32.10.1.en: He who fears the Lord accepts teaching, and those who rise early to Him obtain His favor [14].

32.10.2.en: God stretches out His hand all the day long (Isa 65:2); everyone who rises early to Him and seeks Him earnestly finds Him, for he offers Him the firstfruits, and so obtains His favor. "I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me" (Prov 8:17).

32.10.3.en: He who seeks the Law is filled with it, but the hypocrite stumbles in it [15].

32.10.4.en: He connects indirectly the fear of the Lord with the seeking of the Law, for he says that the fear of the Lord prepares the believer to accept teaching, and goes on to say that he who seeks the Law is filled with it, and so becomes godly, a fearer of the Lord, and not a hypocrite [15]. The hypocrite here means one who knows the Law and deliberately ignores it in his thought, heart and conduct, even if he practices some outward show of religion. In the age of Ben Sirach some of the Jews boasted of the Law and kept it by heart but did not live it.

32.10.5.en: Those who fear the Lord discover (right) judgment, and like light they make righteous works shine [16].

32.10.6.en: In a wonderful sequence and marvelous connection Ben Sirach begins with the divine fear that grants the Lord's favor and His pleasure in His children [14]; the fruit of that is the believer's longing to enjoy the sweetness of the Law and to be filled with it without stumbling, which the hypocrite does not enjoy [15]. By this the fearer of the Lord enters into new depths, and discovers the beauty of discernment and prudence, and practices works of righteousness through divine grace like a light that shines from his depths [16].

32.10.7.en: The sinful man rejects correction, and finds arguments that suit his desire [17].

32.10.8.en: The wise man is constantly concerned with the correction of himself, but the careless sinner ignores it.

32.10.9.en: * It is written in Jeremiah: "Jerusalem hath grievously sinned; therefore she has become a tumult; all that honoured her despise her, because they have seen her nakedness" (Mk 11:8). At any rate, he lessens the severity and harshness of the accusation, showing the sweetness of his teacher, saying: "My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; neither be weary of his correction: for whom the Lord loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth" (Prov 3:11-12), while "the sinful man avoids reproof" [17]. Therefore the Scripture says: "Let the righteous man rebuke me and discipline me, but let not the oil of sinners anoint my head" (Ps 141:5) [9].

32.10.10.en: St. Clement of Alexandria The man of counsel does not neglect thinking, but the stranger and the proud do not tremble in fear [18].

32.11.0.en: Do nothing without counsel, and you will not regret your deed [19].

32.11.1.en: The man who is earnest about the salvation of his soul takes care to think deeply on the Law. And he accepts the counsel of the prudent and the wise. The believer's recourse to counsel instills in him a spirit of humility, so that he does not fall into pride.

32.11.2.en: * Brother, the Holy Scripture says: "Do all things with counsel, and without counsel do nothing." When you were acting without counsel but by your own will, you were not striving with your mind. For there is no one who does not need counsel except God alone, who created wisdom. But when you sought to cut off your own desire according to the mind of God and to attain humility, and to take me, your very little brother, as your counselor, you stirred up the envy of Satan, the enemy of good, who envies all men continually [10].

32.11.3.en: * If you have not yet attained the spiritual level, and are still on the bodily level, humble your mind and submit to your teacher, so that he may teach you with tenderness, and "without counsel do nothing," even if it seems good to you, because the light of Satan is revealed at the end to be darkness. So if you hear or think or see something without the least effort in your heart, know that this is from Satan [11].

32.11.4.en: Sts. Barsanuphius and John * Question: The Lord commands: "Whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain" (Mt 5:41). And the Apostle teaches us to submit ourselves one to another in the fear of Christ (Eph 5:21). Are we then bound to obey everyone, any person who gives us orders?

32.11.5.en: Answer: The matter differs according to those who give the command; they must not wrong the obedience of those who receive the command. Moses did not refuse to listen to his father-in-law Jethro when he gave him good counsel (Ex 18:19). But surely there is no small difference in commands, for some give commands against the commandments of the Lord, and others corrupt the commandments of the Lord, falsifying them in various ways by mixing them with forbidden things, and others give commands that agree with the commandment. Others again, although they do not clearly agree with the commandment, nevertheless contribute and help toward carrying it out. It is therefore necessary to remember the commandment of the Apostle who says: "Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. Abstain from all appearance of evil" (1 Thess 5:20-21). Again he says: "Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ" (2 Cor 10:5). Thus if we are commanded to do something that agrees with the commandments of the Lord, or contributes to fulfilling them, or supports the soul, we must accept the command with zeal and care according to the will of God, and so fulfill what is written: "Bearing with one another in the love of Christ" (Eph 4:20).

32.11.6.en: But if we are commanded to do something against the commandments of the Lord, or something that appears to corrupt or falsify the commandment, then it is time to say: "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29), and to remember the Lord who says: "A stranger will they not follow, but will flee from him: for they know not the voice of strangers" (Jn 10:5).

32.11.7.en: It befits us to take into account the Apostle, who wished to reassure us again, and ventured to speak even of angels, saying: "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed" (Gal 1:8).

32.11.8.en: From these sayings we learn that even if a person is very dear to us, and perhaps in a high position and an object of admiration, yet makes known to us what our Lord requires, or commands us to do something that the Lord forbids, this person must be rejected, and condemned by all who love the Lord [12].

32.11.9.en: St. Basil the Great * The hasty destroy every good deed, and fall into evil because of their lack of discernment of good works. Such people do not think about what they are doing nor when they are doing it. They do not realize that something should not have been done until after its time had passed. To these Ben Sirach addresses his fitting saying: "Do nothing without counsel, and you will not regret your deed" (cf. Sir 32:19). And (Solomon) also says: "(Let thine eyes look right on,) and let thine eyelids look straight before thee" (Prov 4:25). And this does not come to pass unless counsel precedes our deeds. And those who do not examine their deeds go forward, but with closed eyes. These fall quickly where they have neglected the eyelids of counsel, and their feet slip [13].

32.12.0.en: Do not walk in a way full of obstacles, and do not stumble on stony ground [20].

32.13.0.en: Do not trust excessively in a way that has not been examined [21].

32.13.1.en: The wise man avoids ways full of stumblingblocks. And at the same time he must walk with caution, lest there be hidden stumblingblocks [20-21].

32.15.0.en: In all your works entrust yourself to the Lord, for that is the keeping of the commandments [23].

32.15.1.en: * Question: Does the Word permit us to do what is good as each of us pleases?

32.15.2.en: Answer: He who pleases himself pleases a man, because each one of us is a human being. But then "cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm," and this is plain in him who trusts in himself. And there is added: "and whose soul (heart) departeth from the Lord" (Jer 17:5).

32.15.3.en: So he who pleases another, or does something to satisfy himself, falls from godliness, and falls into wavering for human benefit. The Lord says: "But all their works they do for to be seen of men" (Mt 23:5; 6:2). And the Apostle confesses: "For if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). But there is a more serious threat that the Holy Book of God presents, saying: "God has scattered the bones of those who please men (Ps 52:6) LXX [14].

32.16.0.en: St. Basil the Great He who trusts in the Law gives heed to the commandments, and he who trusts in the Lord suffers no loss [24].

32.16.1.en: * What is hard, or painful, or impossible in the Lord's saying: "Sell that thou hast, and give to the poor"? If He had charged you to plow the land or to venture in trade, and to bear the labors that follow from it, you would understand the grief that comes over you; but He offers you the gaining of eternal happiness in an easy way, without work or sweat, so why do you not rejoice in the ease of salvation, instead of lamenting and exposing yourself to the loss of the reward for your work?

32.16.2.en: So if you have not truly killed, as you say, nor stolen, nor borne false witness, you make all your efforts vain, when you do not add to that what can open to you the Kingdom of God. If a physician came to you to set right one of your members, you would not hesitate but would accept it willingly; why then do you grieve and are troubled when the Physician of souls comes to you, wishing to make you perfect by adding to you what you essentially lack?

32.16.3.en: There is no doubt that you are very far from what the love of neighbor requires, and you bear false witness that you love him as yourself.

32.16.4.en: What the Lord offers you is conclusive proof of your lack of true love. For if you had truly kept from your youth the commandment of love for your neighbor, and made yourself equal to your brother, could you have this vast wealth? Care for the poor calls for great expense, if we wish each one of them to receive what is necessary, and all men to benefit from the good things of the earth and obtain what meets their need. For he who loves his neighbor as himself ought not to have more than his brother.

32.16.5.en: It is certain that you have wide possessions, so from where did this inequality arise, if not from your preferring your personal enjoyment at the expense of the happiness of others? The more you increase in riches, the more you fall short in love. If you had loved your neighbor, you would long ago have distributed a part of your money. But you cling to these goods as you cling to a part of your spirit. And it pains you to be deprived of them as it pains you to have a member of your body cut off [15].

32.16.6.en: St. Basil the Great Inspired by Sirach 32

32.17.s.en: Let my life be a banquet that does not cease

32.17.0.en: * Your divine presence turns my life into a feast that does not end.

32.17.1.en: What banquet satisfies our souls with joy like Your presence in us?!

32.17.2.en: You lead the banquet with Your love and Your care, You who in Your humility take the last place.

32.17.3.en: Your presence on any occasion makes our banquets a fountain of joy, delight and holiness!

32.17.4.en: You give the elders wisdom and a word, and You draw the young to Your Word.

32.17.5.en: You pour the wine of Your love into our hearts, so that our souls are made drunk, and our hearts and minds are lifted up to Your heavens!

32.17.6.en: * Your presence stirs in us the spirit of wise leadership, so that our conduct is the best language in which we express our attachment to You!

32.17.7.en: You shine with Your light, O Sun of Righteousness, like lightning, and Your voice thunders, shattering every evil in us!

32.17.8.en: We often count our parties a waste of time, but Your banquet blesses every moment as though it were glorious and fruitful years.

32.17.9.en: * At every celebration and banquet we are bound to return quickly home for the sake of our children's feelings.

32.17.10.en: In Your celebration we set out as to our heavenly home, we set out with our children to You, that all may rest in Your bosom!

32.17.11.en: At Your party the heavenly ones, with the fathers, prophets and apostles, play the quiet music of the Spirit.

32.17.12.en: Your Holy Spirit reveals to us the sweetness of Your commandments!

32.17.13.en: The food of Your banquet is heavenly and exceedingly wonderful.
